newsitem.title: USA: GFOA plans to stick with "yield burning" proposal.
newsitem.headline: GFOA plans to stick with "yield burning" proposal.

text.p: The GFOA will not withdraw a controversial recommendation that dealers disclose price markups on U.S. Treasury securities sold to states and localities despite heavy Wall Street opposition, an official of the group said Tuesday.

Catherine Spain, chief lobbyist for the Government Finance Officers Association, said that objections raised by Public Securities Association officials at an Internal Revenue Service hearing on October 24 were exaggerated and uncompelling.
"We still like the proposal. We are not withdrawing it," Spain said in a telephone interview with Reuters.
Spain was referring to the GFOA's response to an IRS draft rule issued June 26.

Under the rule, localities that get three bona fide bids from dealers that have no material interest in the offerings would enjoy a "rebuttable presumption" that the securities were bought at fair market value.

GFOA countered that getting three bids takes too long and recommended that dealers simply certify to issuers that they sold the Treasuries to them at fair market value. Dealers should disclose the price markup in the process.
Issuers that follow that procedure would enjoy a "safe harbor" from IRS action, under GFOA's plan.
But bond dealers told IRS on October 24 that many of them will not sell Treasury securities to state and local governments if they have to disclose markups.
"It is virtually unheard of that dealers would provide markup data," Michael Decker, a PSA vice president warned IRS officials.
But Spain said, "We've heard this argument before. It's a little bit like the boy who cries wolf."
The bottom line is that dealers "don't want to disclose," Spain said. She added, however, that dealers already are required to know what the markup is and whether it is excessive.
"Why collect the information if it is not going to be available," Spain said.
Spain said some of the more sophisticated issuers around the country have started asking dealers about markups so they can negotiate the amount. "It's a good practice," she said.
"This brings into the open something that issuers probably ought to be asking for already," Spain said.
